title: Brute-force attacks
starter: Estimate how many guesses a computer would need to find a 4-digit PIN, then a 6-letter lower-case password. What does that tell you about password length?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: What is a brute-force attack?
facts: Software tries every possible combination of characters until it finds the password.
No clever trick is needed: just speed, and modern computers are very fast.
It's often automated and aimed at thousands of accounts at once.
stations.challenge: Why is a brute-force attack described as 'trial and error'?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Software tries every possible combination of characters until it finds the password.
Also credit: No clever trick is needed: just speed, and modern computers are very fast.

questions.a: Trying huge numbers of possible passwords until the right one is found

questions.q: Which account is most at risk from brute force?
questions.a: One with a short password made only of lower-case letters

stations.name: Dictionary attacks
facts: A dictionary attack tries lists of common passwords and real words first.
Lists from previous data breaches are used, because people reuse passwords.
'password', '123456' and 'qwerty' are tried within the first second.
stations.challenge: Why is 'Liverpool2015' a weaker password than it looks?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A dictionary attack tries lists of common passwords and real words first.
Also credit: Lists from previous data breaches are used, because people reuse passwords.

questions.q: How is a dictionary attack different from pure brute force?
questions.a: It tries likely words and known passwords first, instead of every combination

questions.q: Why is reusing a password across sites dangerous?
questions.a: If one site is breached, attackers try the same password everywhere else

stations.name: How long would it take?
facts: Each extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords.
Using upper case, numbers and symbols increases the choices per character.
A short password can fall in seconds; a long passphrase could take centuries.
stations.challenge: Use the starter site to test a password you don't use. How could you improve it?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Each extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords.
Also credit: Using upper case, numbers and symbols increases the choices per character.

questions.q: Which password is hardest to brute-force?
Why does adding one character make such a difference?
questions.a: Every extra character multiplies the number of possible combinations

stations.name: Password policies
facts: Organisations set rules: a minimum length, a mix of character types, and no reuse.
Passphrases of three random words are long, strong and memorable.
Password managers create and store a different strong password for every site.
stations.challenge: Write three rules for a school password policy, and explain each.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Organisations set rules: a minimum length, a mix of character types, and no reuse.
Also credit: Passphrases of three random words are long, strong and memorable.

questions.q: Which of these belong in a strong password policy? Select all that apply.
questions.a: A minimum length of at least 12 characters; A mix of letters, numbers and symbols; A different password for each account; Never sharing passwords

questions.q: Why do experts recommend a password manager?
questions.a: It creates and remembers a different strong password for every site

stations.name: Fighting back
facts: Account lockouts: after a few failed attempts the account is locked or delayed.
Two-factor authentication means a stolen password isn't enough.
Rate limiting slows down repeated attempts from the same source.
stations.challenge: Why does a delay of a few seconds after a failed login make brute force much harder?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Account lockouts: after a few failed attempts the account is locked or delayed.
Also credit: CAPTCHA tests block automated software.

questions.q: How does an account lockout stop brute force?
questions.a: The attacker can only make a few guesses before the account is locked

questions.q: Why does two-factor authentication help even if a password is guessed?
questions.a: The attacker also needs the second factor, such as a code on the user's phone

stations.name: Behind the scenes
facts: Websites should store a hash of your password, not the password itself.
Hashing is one-way: you can check a password, but not work it out from the hash.
A 'salt' adds random data so identical passwords have different hashes.
stations.challenge: Why is it serious if a website stores passwords as plain text?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Websites should store a hash of your password, not the password itself.
Also credit: Hashing is one-way: you can check a password, but not work it out from the hash.

questions.q: What should a website store instead of your password?
Why is hashing described as one-way?
questions.a: You can turn a password into a hash, but you can't turn a hash back into the password

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
